Telle said the service must return to its original purpose: controlling and securing land, which he said is fundamental to human fulfillment. Telle’s insight comes less than a week after the Army published new operational warfighting guidance. “Our ability to control and secure that piece of dirt is the ultimate deterrent,” Telle said. “And that's why the Army is the foundation of the joint force, because all strategic power begins and ends where humanity lives, on the land.” The acting secretary also announced that the Army will host its first “Manufacturing Rodeo” in early 2027, including a competition among industrial base partners. He added that the Army will test and evaluate manufacturing processes for weaknesses. “We're going to stress test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes, and see where it breaks,” Telle said. “We're going to learn by doing, not by sitting around postulating at the Pentagon; we're going to find the weak links. We're going to make them stronger, and we're going to keep iterating.” To reiterate the importance of the American Soldier’s role in U.S. conflicts, Telle was joined on stage by Soldiers in uniforms from different eras, including World War II, the Vietnam War, and the Global War on Terror – highlighting the accelerating pace of military innovation over time. To ensure our Soldiers have every competitive advantage on the battlefield, Telle said the Army must leverage “America’s greatest strategic advantages.” The first advantage is the “radical notion, embedded in the American DNA, that human greatness and fulfillment are proportional to human freedom.” The second is America’s unparalleled spirit of innovation, “forged into the hearts of our people as they conquered the punishing dirt of the American frontier.” The third advantage is the nation’s deep and efficient capital markets, where resources naturally rush to fund the next big idea. Telle said the service needs to build adaptable and symbiotic relationships with both industry and service partners to maintain a strategic advantage over the nation’s adversaries. The Army is moving to implement autonomy and robotic capabilities to enhance Soldier lethality. Early this month, Telle announced the establishment of a new command, U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, to accelerate delivery of autonomous technology to Soldiers in six formation areas: armor, fires, sustainment, aviation, combat engineer and training. The new command builds on Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s mandate to implement more autonomous technology into the War Department’s formations. The Army also published new operational warfighting guidance on Oct. 7, titled “How the Army Fights.” The framework outlines how the Army will organize and equip its forces, with greater emphasis on the forward positioning of deployed Soldiers.
